posts.title: Critique the experience someone is having
posts.caption:
A design critique gets more useful when someone describes what the customer is trying to do and how the screen might make that moment feel.

Take a hypothetical checkout. A customer is checking the delivery address before paying. A large urgent button, a hidden total and an ambiguous back link create a very different conversation from a clear order summary with an obvious way to correct a mistake.

I'd ask the team to walk through that decision before collecting visual references. Which information helps someone feel ready to continue? What can they still change? Where does the product need to slow down?

Those answers give the visual direction a job. They also give the team something more useful to discuss than whether a layout feels premium.

If your product experience and brand promise feel disconnected, I would welcome a conversation about the decision your team is working through.

posts.title: Founding designer conversations
posts.caption:
I'm open to founding designer conversations with early-stage teams.

My background spans 11 years across creative direction, product design, startup founding and brand strategy. I want to bring that range to a team while the product's basic decisions are still open.

I'd want to understand the customer problem, what the business needs to prove and the experience people should have when they use the product. From there, the work might be a rough flow, a visual direction or a prototype that helps the team settle a disagreement.

I care about how those pieces hold together. The product's language, behavior and appearance all give people reasons to trust it, or reasons to hesitate.

If your early-stage team is shaping its product and design foundations, I would welcome a conversation about the role.

posts.title: The emotional work of an empty state
posts.caption:
An empty search result can make someone wonder whether the product has lost their work.

Imagine a project library with no matches after a filter is applied. The person may have spent hours on those files. A bare No results message leaves them to work out whether the files are gone, the search failed or the filter is too narrow.

I'd keep the active filters visible, explain what was searched and offer a direct way back to all projects. If the search itself failed, the screen should say that clearly.

The visual treatment needs to support the same explanation. An illustration of an empty box might suggest there is no work at all, which would be the wrong story in this example.

I want the person to understand what happened and feel able to recover. What does your product say when someone's work seems to disappear?
